periods.activity_title: From Queen Victoria's Promise to Colonial Reality
materials: Textbook chapter 9
Printed copy or projected image of Victoria's 1858 proclamation excerpts
Blank two-column chart paper for each group
periods.visual_aids: Illustrated 1850–1950 timeline from the chapter's opening pages projected or drawn on the board

time_bands.activity: Direct students' attention to the chapter's opening timeline on the board. Ask them to read it silently and then identify three events they can place in order and one event they know nothing about. Take two or three responses to build a shared sense of what this chapter will cover, then pose the chapter's opening question: how did a land of diverse geographies, languages and religions come together to end nearly two centuries of British rule?

Read aloud or project two or three sentences from Victoria's 1858 proclamation — its promise to respect the rights and dignity of the native princes and its assurance of equal treatment and no imposition of Christianity. Ask students: what does an official royal proclamation suggest about how the new rulers wanted to be seen? Then share the chapter's account of what actually happened — Residents interfering in princely administration, missionary activity continuing, heavy land taxes producing famines, the 1878 Arms Act barring Indians from keeping arms, British-majority juries lenient towards European crimes. Ask: what is the gap between the promise and the practice, and who paid the price for it?

Students work in groups of three. Each group receives a two-column chart headed 'Victoria's Proclamation Said' and 'Colonial Policy Did'. They draw evidence from the proclamation extract and the chapter section to fill both columns, then write one sentence at the bottom explaining which group of Indians experienced the sharpest contradiction between promise and reality and why. Groups share their bottom-line sentence with the class; the teacher notes points of agreement and disagreement on the board.

Whole-class debrief: the teacher draws together the board notes into a short synthesis, highlighting that racial discrimination was not incidental but systematic — embedded in law (Arms Act, Vernacular Press Act), in pay structures and in access to public spaces. Students jot one question they still have about why the British structured colonial rule this way; two or three are read aloud to frame curiosity for the sections ahead.

periods.section_context: Crown takeover 1858, Victoria's proclamation, racial discrimination laws, famines
periods.teacher_notes: The chapter opens with the 1858 Crown takeover as a hinge moment that reshaped all subsequent Indian experience; use the proclamation text as the unit's anchor document so the analysis stays grounded in a real source rather than generalisation. A common confusion is treating the proclamation's assurances as sincere policy rather than as a political statement designed to stabilise the empire after 1857 — steer students to notice the gap between language and law. Encourage students to name specific laws (Arms Act, Vernacular Press Act) in their group charts so the discrimination feels concrete, not abstract.

competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can interrogate an official colonial proclamation to identify the gap between stated promises and actual policy.

competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can categorise the systematic forms of racial and economic discrimination embedded in colonial law and explain their cumulative social effect.

periods.activity_title: Reformers, Poets and Monks: Feeding the Nationalist Spirit
materials: Textbook chapter 9
Reformers table from the chapter (Brahmo Samaj, Arya Samaj, Shuddhi Movement, Phule, Vidyasagar)
Index card per student
periods.visual_aids: Portrait images of Raja Ram Mohan Roy, Swami Dayananda Saraswati and Swami Vivekananda projected or displayed on the board

time_bands.activity: Display the portraits of Ram Mohan Roy, Dayananda Saraswati and Vivekananda and ask: what challenge is each of these figures responding to? Give students two minutes to write a hypothesis on their index card, then share briefly. Introduce the idea that the nineteenth century saw two simultaneous debates — one about Indian society's internal problems and one about India's place in the world — and that this unit explores both.

Students read the reformers table in their textbooks and then fill in three columns on the back of their index card: the name of the movement, the social practice it challenged, and the alternative it proposed. After three minutes of silent reading and noting, pairs compare their cards. Focus a brief whole-class discussion on this question: the Brahmo Samaj looked to European models for change while the Arya Samaj said 'return to the Vedas' — are these two different kinds of answer to the same problem? What does each say about where authority for change should come from?

Move to the 'Other Influences' section. The teacher reads aloud the passage on Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay and Bande Mataram — composed 1875, sung at the 1896 Congress session, adopted as National Song in 1950 — then asks: this poem travelled from a novel set in an eighteenth-century famine to an independence movement a century later. What does that journey tell us about how cultural symbols persist through political change? Then read the passage on Vivekananda's 1893 Chicago speech and his call 'Arise, awake, and stop not till the goal is reached.' Ask students: what fear was Vivekananda addressing, and how does naming it publicly change anything?

Students write a four-sentence reflection on their index card: (1) one reform movement and the social practice it challenged, (2) one cultural figure and the symbol or idea they contributed, (3) the connection between these two streams, and (4) one question they would ask any of these figures if they could. Two or three are read aloud.

periods.section_context: Brahmo Samaj, Arya Samaj, Vivekananda, Bande Mataram origins, Anandamath
periods.teacher_notes: Having examined the structural conditions of colonial rule, this unit turns to the intellectual and cultural currents that gave Indians the confidence to resist — the connection is important but should emerge from the content rather than be stated as a formula. A frequent confusion is treating the reform movements as purely religious, missing their social dimension (widow rights, girls' education, caste discrimination); help students see each movement's social target explicitly. Vivekananda's Chicago speech is sometimes read as mere cultural pride — push students to notice his practical advice (encourage science, found institutions) alongside his civilisational argument.

competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can connect social reform initiatives and cultural currents to the broader shift in nationalist consciousness.

competency_edges.competency_text: Identify continuities in cultural and civilisational traditions across periods of political change.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can identify how cultural symbols and spiritual traditions carried forward across political changes to sustain nationalist consciousness.

competency_edges.competency_text: Recognise India's contributions to global knowledge and civilisation and their significance.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can articulate how Indian thinkers presented their civilisational traditions to a global audience and explain the domestic confidence this generated.

periods.activity_title: The Congress, the Crowd and the Underground
periods.section_anchor: The Rise of the Indian National Congress / Growing Discontent
materials: Textbook chapter 9
Role cards for four groups: Congress leadership, Kuka movement, Chapekar brothers/Tilak strand, Birsa Munda/tribal resistance

time_bands.activity: Pose this question to the class: in 1885 the Indian National Congress held its first session in Bombay with seventy-two delegates passing polite resolutions. In 1900, Birsa Munda died in jail after leading an armed uprising against colonial authority. Were these two things part of the same story? Give students two minutes to write yes or no and a reason, then take three or four responses to surface the range of thinking before reading begins.

Students read the two sections silently. Then distribute role cards: Group A is the Congress leadership (Hume, Naoroji, Bonnerjee) expressing full faith in British rule while seeking dialogue; Group B is the Kuka movement of Baba Ram Singh — white hand-spun clothes, rejection of foreign goods, private courts, sixty-five followers blown from cannons; Group C is the Tilak strand — Kesari newspaper, Ganesh Chaturthi as a political festival, sedition charge, 'Lokmanya'; Group D is Birsa Munda's 'Ulgulaaan' against landlords, missionaries and colonial authority. Each group reads their card, then prepares two sentences: what strategy are we using, and what does the colonial government's response tell us about what the British feared most?

Groups present their two sentences. The teacher facilitates a structured comparison: ask the class — which strategy reached the most people? Which provoked the harshest response? Which built lasting institutions? Record answers on the board in three columns. Then ask: if all four approaches existed at the same time, does it make sense to call any one of them 'the' independence movement?

Students write a closing argument of three sentences: which approach — Congress petitions, cultural mobilisation, direct action, or armed uprising — do they judge most effective at this stage of the struggle, and on what grounds? The teacher notes that historians still debate this; the point is not a single correct answer but a reasoned one grounded in evidence from the sections.

periods.section_context: INC founding 1885, Namdhari movement, Chapekar brothers, Tilak, Birsa Munda
periods.teacher_notes: The Congress's profession of 'unswerving allegiance to the British Crown' at its founding is often read by students as weakness or collaboration; help them see it as a strategic choice within a specific power context, then contrast it with the Kuka movement's entirely different strategic logic. A common confusion is treating 'Growing Discontent' as merely a list of violent acts rather than as evidence of diverse popular grievances — each episode (Kukas, Chapekar brothers, Birsa Munda) has a distinct social base and a distinct cause. The role-play structure keeps the comparison concrete; insist students name the strategy, not just the person.

competency_edges.competency_text: Explain and analyse major changes in the past and their impact on society.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can assess how organised political forums and grassroots resistance together changed the landscape of anti-colonial action.

competency_edges.competency_text: Assess the influence of political institutions on Indian society.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can assess the reach and limitations of the early Congress as a political institution in representing diverse Indian grievances.

periods.activity_title: Divide and Resist: The Partition of Bengal and Its Aftermath
periods.section_anchor: The 1905 Partition of Bengal and National Awakening
materials: Textbook chapter 9
Outline map of Bengal showing the proposed partition line
Cause-effect diagram template (blank boxes and arrows) per student
periods.visual_aids: Simple map showing Bengal divided into largely Muslim east and largely Hindu west, projected or drawn on board

time_bands.activity: Show the outline map of Bengal and explain that in 1905 Viceroy Curzon announced the partition of the Bengal presidency, officially for administrative efficiency. Ask students: if you were a senior British official in 1905 and wanted to weaken a province that was becoming politically active, how might you draw the boundary? Give them a moment to mark a hypothetical line on their maps and share reasoning.

Students read the section. Then the teacher explains what Curzon actually did: split the largely Muslim east from the largely Hindu west, a classic application of 'divide and rule'. Ask: who supported the partition and why? (Most Muslim leaders defended it, since the new eastern province gave Muslims a majority.) Who opposed it and how? (Tagore, Banerjee, Bipin Pal — meetings, processions, the singing of Vande Mataram in the streets, tying of rakhis as Hindu-Muslim solidarity.) What did the colonial government do when Vande Mataram became too politically charged? (Banned it in the streets.)

Students complete a cause-effect diagram on the template provided. In the cause box: Curzon's partition decision and its stated vs actual purpose. In two separate effect boxes: (a) the sharpened communal division it produced, and (b) the national awakening — Swadeshi, boycott, rakhi-tying, protests. Below the diagram, students write one sentence: which effect do you judge more significant for the long-term future of the independence movement, and why?

Pairs exchange diagrams, read each other's one-sentence judgement, and write one challenge or supporting point on their partner's sheet. A few exchanges are read aloud. The teacher closes by noting that the annulment of the partition in 1911 is part of the next strand of the story, and that the communal division the partition sharpened did not disappear with the annulment.

periods.section_context: Curzon's partition, Swadeshi, boycott, rakhi, Vande Mataram in streets
pedagogical_approaches: Some specific opportunities for projects to create models and artefacts
periods.teacher_notes: The key analytical move in this unit is distinguishing the stated reason for partition (administrative efficiency) from its actual purpose (divide and rule), and then tracing two simultaneous and contradictory effects; help students hold both effects in mind rather than collapsing the section into either a simple unity story or a simple division story. Students often confuse Swadeshi with boycott — Swadeshi is the positive embrace of Indian-made goods, boycott is the active rejection of foreign ones; the two programmes are related but distinct. The Jamsetji Tata Swadeshi Mills reference (1886) is useful for showing students that Swadeshi thinking predated the 1905 crisis.

competency_edges.competency_text: Explain and analyse major changes in the past and their impact on society.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can analyse how a colonial administrative decision triggered a new phase of mass political mobilisation.

competency_edges.competency_text: Explain the reasons behind harmony and conflict among communities and their impact on society.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can explain how a deliberate colonial strategy of communal division simultaneously produced both inter-community solidarity and lasting antagonism.

competency_edges.competency_text: Identify continuities in cultural and civilisational traditions across periods of political change.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can trace how a cultural symbol composed decades earlier was reactivated as a vehicle for political resistance.

periods.activity_title: Reading the Bande Mataram: A Four-Point Programme Takes Shape
materials: Textbook chapter 9
Projected or printed image of the Bande Mataram daily front page (from textbook)
Printed extract from the September 1906 article on 'absolute national autonomy'
periods.visual_aids: Front page of the Bande Mataram daily as reproduced in the textbook, projected for whole-class viewing

time_bands.activity: Project the front page of the Bande Mataram daily and ask students to observe it silently for one minute: what do they notice about the boxes on either side of the title, the language used, the name of the publication itself? Take observations without correcting or confirming — students are practising close reading of a historical document before any explanation is given.

Read aloud the September 1906 extract: the agitation is not merely against the Partition but for 'absolute national autonomy'. Ask: why might the editors have written 'absolute national autonomy' instead of simply 'independence'? What political risk does the word 'independence' carry in 1906 that 'autonomy' avoids? Students discuss in pairs, then share. The teacher explains the context: Bipin Pal launched the paper, Aurobindo Ghose took charge, and the paper added National Education to Swadeshi and boycott to form a four-point programme. In December 1906 the Calcutta Congress session, under Dadabhai Naoroji, formally adopted all four as Congress objectives — though 'Swaraj' was left deliberately undefined.

Students work individually on a structured source analysis: (1) What is the main claim of the September 1906 extract? (2) What evidence in the extract suggests the writers are thinking beyond just opposing the Bengal partition? (3) Why might leaving 'Swaraj' undefined have been a strategic advantage in 1906? (4) The paper was published in English — who was its intended audience, and what does that tell us about the movement's strategy? Students write answers in their notebooks.

Three or four students share their answer to question 3 or 4 — the more analytical questions. The teacher draws the discussion to a close by connecting the four-point programme (Swaraj, Swadeshi, boycott, National Education) to the earlier Swadeshi and boycott responses to partition, showing how a reactive protest hardened into a coherent political agenda within a year.

periods.section_context: Bande Mataram daily, Swaraj, Swadeshi, boycott, National Education, Calcutta Congress 1906
periods.teacher_notes: The Bande Mataram daily extract is a genuine primary source and the source-analysis questions should be kept demanding — students who only paraphrase the extract are not yet interpreting it. A recurring confusion is equating 'Swaraj' with 'independence from the start': the section is explicit that Swaraj ranged in meaning from self-rule within the Empire to full independence, and the ambiguity was deliberate. The National Council of Education and Bengal National College with Aurobindo as principal are concrete institutional expressions of the programme and worth naming so the agenda does not seem merely rhetorical.

competency_edges.competency_text: Explain and analyse major changes in the past and their impact on society.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can explain how the articulation of a four-point nationalist programme changed the character of the independence movement.

competency_edges.competency_text: Interpret primary and secondary sources to construct historical understanding.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can read a period newspaper extract to decode the political language used to advance nationalist goals.

periods.activity_title: The Surat Split: When a Movement Breaks in Two
materials: Textbook chapter 9
Position brief cards for two groups: Moderates and Nationalists

time_bands.activity: Write on the board: 'Extremist'. 'Radical'. 'Nationalist'. Tell students these three words were applied to the same group of people at the Surat Congress in December 1907. Ask: who gets to name a political movement — those inside it or those outside it? And why does the name matter? Brief discussion to surface the idea that political labels carry power before the content is introduced.

Students read the section. The teacher then summarises the context: the British authorities, alarmed by the Calcutta session's call for Swaraj, pressured the Moderate faction — Naoroji, Gokhale, Pherozeshah Mehta, Surendranath Banerjee, Rashbehari Ghosh — to step back from the Calcutta resolutions and return to requests for gradual self-government within the Empire. When Tilak was prevented from speaking, the session collapsed into chaos; the Nationalist camp — Tilak, Lala Lajpat Rai ('Lion of Punjab'), Aurobindo Ghose — walked out to hold a separate session.

Distribute position brief cards. Moderates group prepares answers to: what do you want, what is your timeline, and what risk does pushing too fast create? Nationalists group prepares: what do you want, what is your timeline, and what risk does going too slow create? Each group also prepares one question to ask the other side. Groups face each other and exchange questions and answers for approximately eight minutes, with the teacher as facilitator.

Come out of role. The teacher asks the whole class: after this split, which institutional form of the independence movement was stronger, and which was weaker? What does a split like this do to a movement's ability to negotiate with a colonial power? Students write one concluding sentence. The teacher closes by noting that the split was not permanent — the question of how the factions might reunite is carried forward by the content of the next chapter sections.

periods.section_context: Moderates vs Nationalists, Tilak silenced, walkout, labels Extremist vs Nationalist
periods.teacher_notes: The core analytical task is understanding the Surat split as an institutional rupture with strategic consequences, not merely a personal quarrel; keep students focused on what each faction wanted and why the British preferred the Moderate position. Students often assume the Nationalists were simply 'right' and the Moderates wrong — push them to articulate the Moderates' strategic logic (incremental gains reduce risk, maintain elite support) before evaluating it. The labelling question raised in the opening move is important: the chapter is explicit that the group called 'Extremists' by their opponents called themselves 'Nationalists', and that asymmetry tells students something about who controls political discourse.

competency_edges.competency_text: Explain and analyse major changes in the past and their impact on society.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can analyse how an organisational rupture reshaped the strategies available to the independence movement.

competency_edges.competency_text: Assess the influence of political institutions on Indian society.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can assess how an institutional split altered the political options available to different factions within the independence movement.

periods.activity_title: Reuniting the Congress: Home Rule, the Lucknow Pact and the Cost of Agreement
periods.section_anchor: Home Rule Movement and the Lucknow Pact
materials: Textbook chapter 9
Short structured discussion prompt printed for each pair

time_bands.activity: Ask the class: after the Surat split, Tilak in jail and two hostile Congress factions, how would you reunite a fractured national movement? Give students two minutes to sketch an answer, then share. Introduce Tilak's three stated tasks after his 1914 release — reunite Congress factions, promote Hindu-Muslim cooperation, work towards home rule — as a way of showing that the problems students named were exactly the ones the actors themselves identified.

Students read the section. The teacher then walks through the 1916 Lucknow session: the two factions of the Congress reunited; the Congress and the All-India Muslim League concluded the Lucknow Pact, in which the Congress accepted separate electorates for Muslims in elections to the legislative councils; Tilak and Annie Besant launched the Home Rule Movement the same year. Ask: what did the Congress give up in the Lucknow Pact? (Acceptance of separate electorates.) What did it hope to gain? (Muslim League support for home rule.) Was that a good trade-off?

Pairs work on the structured discussion prompt: (1) The Lucknow Pact gave Muslim communities separate electorates — does this recognise a legitimate need for representation, or does it entrench communal difference into the political system? (2) Annie Besant was an Irish philosopher and activist, not an Indian — does her nationality strengthen or complicate the Home Rule demand, and why? Pairs write two or three sentences on each question, then share one answer each with the class.

Whole-class reflection: the British refused even home rule — self-government within the Empire. Ask students: if the colonial power won't concede the minimum, what does that tell a political movement about its next step? The teacher notes this as the hinge point the chapter identifies: 'the struggle was poised to enter a new phase of mass political mobilisation.' Students write one sentence naming what they think that next phase will need to look like.

periods.section_context: Tilak and Besant Home Rule, Lucknow Pact, separate electorates, Congress reunification
periods.teacher_notes: The Lucknow Pact is pivotal because it introduced separate electorates into formal Congress policy — a decision that students should interrogate rather than simply note, since the chapter later shows this contributing to communal division. Annie Besant's role tends to surprise students accustomed to reading the independence movement as purely Indian; use that surprise to ask what it means for a colonised people to find allies within the colonising tradition. The Home Rule demand (self-government within the Empire) should be distinguished clearly from Swaraj and Purna Swaraj — the section is explicit that home rule was a 'practical first step', not the final goal.

competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can explain how inter-organisational agreements and new demands altered the direction of the freedom struggle.

periods.activity_title: Mass Mobilisation, Massacre and the Limits of an Alliance
materials: Textbook chapter 9
Printed excerpt from Tagore's letter returning his knighthood
Blank structured-response sheet for the source analysis
periods.visual_aids: Photograph of Gandhi spinning khadi as reproduced in the textbook, projected for whole-class reading

time_bands.activity: Project the photograph of Gandhi spinning khadi and ask: what is this image doing that a speech cannot? Students share observations. Introduce the Rowlatt Act of 1919 — detention without trial, curtailment of civil liberties — as the immediate provocation for Gandhi's nationwide protest, and the Jallianwala Bagh massacre of 13 April 1919 as the event that turned widespread discontent into mass resolve.

The teacher narrates the Jallianwala Bagh massacre: thousands gathered in the garden to celebrate Baisakhi and to protest the arrest of local leaders and the Rowlatt Act; Brigadier-General Dyer sealed the main exit and fired approximately 1,650 rounds, deliberately aiming at the thickest parts of the crowd; official British counts admitted nearly 400 dead and over 1,200 wounded; Indian estimates exceeded 1,000. Then distribute the Tagore letter excerpt. Students read it silently and answer: what does Tagore mean when he says the rulers 'congratulated themselves'? What does returning a knighthood accomplish that a written protest alone might not?

Move to the Khilafat alliance and Non-Cooperation Movement. The teacher explains: Gandhi saw the Khilafat issue as an opportunity for Hindu-Muslim unity and in 1920 forged an alliance between Khilafat leaders and the Congress, merging the movement with Non-Cooperation. Ask students: Jinnah left the Congress at its 1920 session, warning against mixing religion with the independence movement. Was his concern more about strategy or principle? Students discuss in groups of three, then share.

The teacher narrates Chauri Chaura (February 1922) — protesters killed policemen by setting a station on fire; Gandhi called off the movement as 'inhuman conduct' — and the controversy this provoked among leaders including Motilal Nehru, Jawaharlal Nehru, C.R. Das and Subhas Chandra Bose. Ask students: Gandhi withdrew a mass movement because of one violent incident in one village. What does that tell us about the conditions a nonviolent movement places on its own success? Students write one concluding sentence.

periods.section_context: Rowlatt Act, Jallianwala Bagh massacre, Khilafat alliance, Chauri Chaura, movement suspended
periods.teacher_notes: Jallianwala Bagh is often taught as a self-contained atrocity — help students connect it explicitly to the Rowlatt Act protest and to Tagore's source letter, so the source-interpretation task has a real analytical purpose. The Khilafat alliance and its aftermath require careful handling: the temporary unity it produced and the reinforced sense of separateness and subsequent riots it left behind must both be acknowledged, and students should grapple with Jinnah's dissent rather than dismiss it as communalism. Chauri Chaura is a genuine test of Gandhi's principle — the decision to call off a mass movement over one incident was widely contested by leaders the students already know by name, which makes the disagreement concrete rather than abstract.

competency_edges.competency_text: Explain and analyse major changes in the past and their impact on society.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can evaluate how state repression and the withdrawal of mass movements together transformed the pace and method of anti-colonial struggle.

competency_edges.competency_text: Interpret primary and secondary sources to construct historical understanding.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can interpret a protest letter from a public figure to reconstruct the moral and political critique it makes of state violence.

competency_edges.competency_text: Explain the reasons behind harmony and conflict among communities and their impact on society.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can assess the conditions under which a cross-community political alliance forms, fractures, and leaves a contested legacy.

periods.activity_title: Simon Go Back: Repression, Revenge and the Revolutionary Turn
materials: Textbook chapter 9
Short scenario card for each group describing one episode: Simon Commission, Lajpat Rai's lathi-charge, Kakori robbery and executions, Bhagat Singh in the Assembly

time_bands.activity: Write on the board: 'The deaf must hear.' Tell students this is how Bhagat Singh described his purpose in dropping low-intensity bombs in Delhi's Central Legislative Assembly in 1929. Ask: what does it mean to do something not for its physical effect but for its symbolic one? Does intent change how we judge an act? Brief discussion to surface the question of means before the content is presented.

Students read the section. Then the teacher distributes scenario cards. Each group reads their episode and prepares answers to: what was the British action that provoked this response? What form did the response take? What did the British do next? What happened to the people involved? Groups have approximately six minutes, then each group presents their episode in two minutes.

The teacher facilitates a structured comparison across the four episodes: in each case, the British action (all-white Simon Commission, brutal lathi-charge of a nonviolent march, arrests and executions of Kakori participants, curtailment of prisoner rights) produced a response that escalated, not de-escalated, the conflict. Ask: what does this pattern of escalation tell us about the British government's political judgement at this stage? Was there a point where a different British decision might have changed the trajectory?

Students write three sentences: (1) one British action from this period and the Indian response it triggered; (2) whether they judge the Indian response as effective, and on what grounds; (3) the name and source of the statement they find most significant from this section — Lajpat Rai's 'last nails in the coffin of British rule' or Bhagat Singh's 'make the deaf hear' — and why. Two or three are read aloud.

periods.section_context: Simon Commission, Lajpat Rai's death, Kakori robbery, Bhagat Singh, Chandrashekar Azad
periods.teacher_notes: The section covers both nonviolent and revolutionary responses to the same colonial policies; keep students from sorting the figures into 'good' and 'bad' categories and instead ask them to engage with the strategic logic each person was following. A frequent confusion is treating Bhagat Singh's Assembly bomb as an assassination attempt — the chapter is explicit that the bombs were low-intensity and the intent was 'to make the deaf hear', not to kill; this distinction matters for interpreting his politics. Suniti Chowdhury, Shanti Ghosh and Bina Das appear here — naming these women freedom fighters explicitly counters the tendency to treat the revolutionary strand as exclusively male.

competency_edges.competency_text: Explain and analyse major changes in the past and their impact on society.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can analyse how British refusal to consult Indians and the resulting repression accelerated demands for complete independence.

competency_edges.competency_text: Assess the influence of political institutions on Indian society.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can evaluate how a colonial institution's deliberate exclusion of Indian voices shaped the character of Indian political resistance.

periods.activity_title: Purna Swaraj: The Salt March, the Pact, and the Poona Agreement
materials: Textbook chapter 9
Printed extract of the Lahore resolution demanding Purna Swaraj
Group analysis worksheet with four guiding questions
periods.visual_aids: Simple map tracing the 380-km Dandi Salt March route, projected or drawn on board

time_bands.activity: Show the Dandi route map and ask: Gandhi chose to walk 380 kilometres to collect salt from the sea. Why salt, out of all possible forms of protest? Give students two minutes to hypothesise, then share. The teacher confirms: the colonial government held a monopoly on salt production and taxed it heavily — salt was something every Indian, however poor, needed every day, and the monopoly made it a direct, daily experience of colonial economic control.

Students read the section. The teacher then distributes the Lahore resolution extract and the group analysis worksheet. Groups of four work through the questions: (1) What exact right does the resolution assert — how specific or general is the language? (2) The resolution says Indians have the right 'to alter or abolish an oppressive government' — where does this idea come from? (3) Why does the resolution use the word 'inalienable'? (4) Compare the demand here with the 'Swaraj' of the 1906 Calcutta session — what has changed and what remains ambiguous? Groups have approximately ten minutes.

Groups share their answers to questions 3 and 4 — the more analytical ones. The teacher then moves to the Gandhi-Irwin Pact (1931): release of political prisoners not involved in violence, limited private salt manufacture allowed, Congress suspends civil disobedience and attends a Round Table Conference. Ask: was this a victory, a compromise, or a retreat? Then the Poona Pact: Gandhi's fast unto death against Ambedkar's position on separate electorates, the replacement of separate electorates with increased reserved seats. Ask: who gave up more in the Poona Pact, and how does each side's position reflect their reading of what political representation is for?

Students write a structured two-paragraph response in their notebooks: paragraph one assesses the Lahore resolution as a political document — what it demands, how it grounds its demand, and how it differs from earlier Congress positions; paragraph two evaluates either the Gandhi-Irwin Pact or the Poona Pact as a case of political negotiation — what each party gained and gave up. Two students read a paragraph each; the class adds a point or challenge.

periods.section_context: Lahore resolution 1929, Dandi Salt March 1930, Gandhi-Irwin Pact, Poona Pact
periods.teacher_notes: The source-analysis of the Lahore resolution is the core task of this unit; make sure groups engage with the exact language of the text rather than summarising it from memory. Students often treat the Gandhi-Irwin Pact as a straightforward victory; the chapter notes it was criticised by younger Congress leaders for not guaranteeing Purna Swaraj and was followed by massive arrests and waning public enthusiasm — both sides of this should appear in discussion. The Ambedkar-Gandhi disagreement over separate electorates is not a footnote — it illustrates a fundamental question about whether political representation for a marginalised community should be integrated or separated, and students should be asked to articulate both positions before judging.

periods.activity_title: Two Nations or One? The Idea of Separate Nations Examined
materials: Textbook chapter 9
Structured comparison table template per student
Short printed quotations: Iqbal's 1930 proposal, Jinnah's endorsement of Pakistan, Maulana Azad's opposition, Savarkar's Hindu Mahasabha position

time_bands.activity: Ask: can two communities share the same land and government, or do deep religious and cultural differences make separate political structures necessary? Give students two minutes to write a position and a reason. Make clear this is a question the chapter takes seriously and examines through specific historical arguments — it is not a question with one obvious answer.

Students read the section. The teacher then introduces each of the four quotations: Iqbal's 1930 proposal for a separate Muslim territory within an Indian federation; Jinnah's endorsement of Pakistan; Azad and Khan's insistence that Hindus and Muslims could live together; Savarkar's Hindu Mahasabha position that Hindus and Muslims were two distinct nations side by side. Each student receives the printed quotations and places them on their comparison table under two headings: 'Argument for separate political arrangements' and 'Argument for shared political arrangements', adding one sentence explaining the reasoning behind each position.

Students discuss in groups of three: (1) Iqbal's 1930 proposal was for a Muslim territory within a larger Indian federation — it was not yet the precise idea of Pakistan. Why does this distinction matter? (2) The chapter says nearly all Congress leaders, including Muslim leaders, opposed the Two-Nation idea. How should we weigh the fact that the idea was endorsed by a minority of leaders against the fact that it ultimately prevailed? (3) What role did the British play in allowing or encouraging Hindu-Muslim differences to grow, according to the chapter? Groups note their key points, then two groups share.

Students write a paragraph comparing two positions from their table — they must name the person, state the argument, identify the assumption behind it, and assess its historical consequence. The teacher closes by noting that the chapter explicitly says whether partition was the only way forward 'has been debated ever since' — this is an open historical question, not a settled one.

periods.section_context: Iqbal's 1930 proposal, Two-Nation idea, Jinnah, Azad and Khan's opposition, Hindu Mahasabha
periods.teacher_notes: Students may arrive with strong prior views on partition; the analytical task is to make them engage with the specific historical arguments in the section rather than projecting present-day positions backward. A common confusion is treating Iqbal's 1930 proposal as equivalent to the Pakistan demand — the chapter is explicit that 'this was not yet the precise idea of Pakistan', and the distinction is historically significant. The Savarkar-Hindu Mahasabha position often surprises students who associate the Two-Nation idea only with the Muslim League — naming it keeps the analysis historically accurate and avoids simplification.

periods.activity_title: Do or Die: The Quit India Movement and the Breaking Point
materials: Textbook chapter 9
Reflective box data on numbers jailed in four movements (Non-Cooperation, Salt Satyagraha, Civil Disobedience, Quit India) projected or printed
periods.visual_aids: Projected data table showing numbers jailed across the four major movements

time_bands.activity: Project the jailed-numbers data table. Ask students: what pattern do you see across the four movements? What does a rising count of arrests tell you about the British government's response to each successive movement — and about the movements' growing reach? Students share observations before any explanation of the Quit India Movement is given.

Students read the section. The teacher then unpacks the context: India was pulled into World War II without being consulted; more than 2.5 million Indian soldiers joined; the Bengal famine of 1943 killed millions while grain was exported on Churchill's orders; Stafford Cripps offered dominion status after the war but with a provision allowing provinces to opt out of post-war India. Gandhi rejected it and in August 1942 launched Quit India with the call 'Do or Die'. Ask students: the Cripps offer included a post-war promise. Why might Gandhi have rejected a future promise rather than accepting it?

The teacher narrates the movement's scale: virtually the entire Congress leadership was arrested; workers struck; students left schools; government buildings were attacked; telegraph poles uprooted; Ram Manohar Lohia and Jayaprakash Narayan kept the underground movement going; Aruna Asaf Ali hoisted the national flag at Gowalia Tank Maidan when senior leaders were arrested and went underground for nearly four years. Viceroy Linlithgow called it 'by far the most serious rebellion since 1857'. Ask: the movement was brutally suppressed and did not immediately win independence. Does that mean it failed? Students discuss in pairs.

Students write a structured evaluation: (1) What did the Congress give up by launching Quit India in wartime? (2) What did the movement demonstrate about the British ability to govern with Indian consent? (3) Viceroy Linlithgow's assessment and the scale of suppression — do these together make the movement a success, a failure, or something more complicated? Students share one sentence from their evaluations; the teacher notes the plurality of readings as itself historically significant.

periods.section_context: Cripps Mission rejected, Do or Die call, mass arrests, underground leaders, Viceroy's assessment
periods.teacher_notes: The Bengal famine of 1943 is often left out of the Quit India story — include it as the context that made 'sacrificing for a war that was not their own' feel viscerally unjust to millions of Indians. A recurring confusion is treating the movement's military suppression as evidence of its failure; the chapter is explicit that it 'signalled that the British could no longer rule India without Indian consent' — help students distinguish military outcome from political consequence. Aruna Asaf Ali and Kanaklata Barua are named in the boxed notes; make space for them rather than letting the narrative default to male leaders.

periods.activity_title: The End of Empire: Mutinies, Deadlock and Direct Action
materials: Textbook chapter 9
Cause-effect map template per group
Short printed passage describing Direct Action Day violence in Calcutta

time_bands.activity: Ask students: by 1945 the British had defeated the Axis powers. Why, at the moment of their greatest military victory, did they choose to leave India? Give students two minutes to hypothesise, then take three or four responses. List the factors students name on the board; return to them at the end of the unit to see which are confirmed and which are revised by the chapter's account.

Students read the first part of the section (up to and including the Cabinet Mission). The teacher then narrates the two mutinies: the Royal Indian Air Force mutiny in January 1946 and the Royal Indian Navy mutiny in February 1946, where naval ratings rebelled against ill-treatment and the revolt spread across India. Ask: what does a mutiny in the armed forces tell the colonial power that a political protest cannot? Then explain the Cabinet Mission's plan — three groups of provinces with complete autonomy except in defence, foreign affairs and communication — and its failure due to deep divisions between the Congress and the Muslim League.

Groups receive a cause-effect map template. They map the following chain: (a) Jinnah's Direct Action Day call of 16 August 1946 and his statement 'We will either have a divided India or a destroyed India'; (b) the wave of communal violence in Calcutta; (c) the deep fear created that made peaceful coexistence seem impossible; (d) the conclusion drawn by British planners about the pace of transfer. Then the teacher reads aloud the Direct Action Day passage and asks: the chapter says the violence was 'encouraged by provocative speeches and pamphlets'. Does that make it planned, spontaneous, or both?

Groups share their maps. The teacher consolidates: the mutinies showed the British they could no longer rely on the Indian military; the Cabinet Mission deadlock showed no agreed political solution was near; Direct Action showed the cost of continued delay. Ask students to revise the board list from the opening move — which factors from their hypotheses appear in the chapter and which do not? Students write one sentence on what they now think was the decisive factor.

periods.section_context: Navy and Air Force mutinies, Cabinet Mission deadlock, Direct Action, Radcliffe Line, princely states
pedagogical_approaches: Some specific opportunities for projects to create models and artefacts
periods.teacher_notes: The military mutinies are often underemphasised in standard accounts focused on Gandhi and the Congress; the chapter explicitly names historians' move away from crediting Britain's exit mainly to those figures, and this unit is the place to give the mutinies their analytical weight. The Direct Action Day violence in Calcutta should be presented with care — the chapter says thousands were killed as Muslim mobs attacked Hindus who then retaliated; the sequence and the retaliation both matter, and simplifying it to one-sided violence distorts the record. The Cabinet Mission's plan is genuinely complex; drawing it on the board as three grouped blocks of provinces with named reservations (defence, foreign affairs, communication) helps students see why the Congress and the League could not agree on what 'autonomy' meant within it.

periods.activity_title: Freedom at Midnight: Independence, Partition and the Long View
materials: Textbook chapter 9
Closing recap section ('Before we move on…') from the chapter
Blank reflection sheet per student
periods.visual_aids: Simple map showing the Radcliffe Line dividing Punjab and Bengal, creating India and the two wings of Pakistan, projected or drawn on board

time_bands.activity: Show the Radcliffe Line map. Tell students: Cyril Radcliffe was a British lawyer who had never been to India. He was given five weeks to draw a line splitting Punjab and Bengal, creating India and a Pakistan comprising West Pakistan and East Pakistan. Ask: what are the predictable consequences of drawing such a boundary in five weeks, for millions of people on both sides? Students list predictions in their notebooks before the teacher presents the chapter's account.

Students read the closing sections of the chapter — the Partition violence, the princely states' integration, the midnight independence declaration — while the teacher adds narrative: millions found themselves on the 'wrong' side of new borders; organised gangs, rumours and a desire to 'cleanse' new territories drove massacres in which women were especially targeted; Gandhi lamented that the violence secretly harboured had come back on the nation. Then explain Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel's integration of more than 560 princely states through persuasion, firmness and, as a last resort, military action. Ask: why is this integration called the work of the 'Iron Man of India' rather than a routine administrative task?

Students read the 'Before we move on…' recap and the closing reflective box listing unnamed freedom fighters. On their reflection sheet they respond to two questions: (1) The recap identifies four approaches to independence — Moderates, Nationalists, revolutionaries, Gandhi's mass nonviolence. Which approach do you judge contributed most to the eventual outcome, and what evidence from the chapter supports your judgement? (2) The chapter asks what sort of nation free India would build. Write one sentence describing what you think that obligation means for someone living in India today. Pairs exchange sheets and add one agreement and one challenge.

Whole-class closing discussion: the teacher reads aloud the chapter's final observation — 'from 1857 to 1947, for ninety years, generations of Indians fought and sacrificed, and India's freedom was a hard-won collective victory.' Ask: historians have moved from crediting Britain's exit mainly to Gandhi and the Congress to recognising multiple factors — popular uprisings, revolutionary attempts, the military mutinies, Britain's post-war diminishment and worldwide decolonisation. Does that broader account make the story bigger or smaller? Students share one word or phrase that captures their reading of the chapter as a whole.

periods.section_context: Partition violence, Patel's integration of princely states, Nehru's midnight speech, decolonisation
periods.teacher_notes: This unit carries the weight of the chapter's closing argument — that 1947 was both triumph and tragedy — and the reflection task should be given genuine time rather than squeezed into a summary. A common confusion is treating Patel's integration of the princely states as automatic or peaceful; the chapter notes military action was used as a last resort, and students should understand that over 560 states with independent rulers choosing among India, Pakistan or technical independence was an enormous and contested process. The closing discussion on multiple factors behind independence is an opportunity to circle back to figures and movements from earlier units — the navy mutiny, Bhagat Singh, Birsa Munda, Aruna Asaf Ali — and to resist the textbook habit of attributing the outcome to one leader or one moment.

competency.competency_text: Explain and analyse major changes in the past and their impact on society.

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can assess how organised political forums and grassroots resistance together changed the landscape of anti-colonial action.
assessment_items.chapter_section: The Rise of the Indian National Congress / Growing Discontent
assessment_items.task: The Indian National Congress held its first session in 1885 with polite resolutions, while in the same decades the Kuka movement, Bal Gangadhar Tilak's cultural mobilisation, and Birsa Munda's Ulgulaaan were also part of the resistance to colonial rule. Create a comparison table that places these four approaches to anti-colonial action side by side, then write a short paragraph (three to four sentences) evaluating which approach you judge most changed what the colonial government feared.
assessment_items.scaffold: Your table should have one row for each approach and four columns: (1) Name of approach / leader; (2) Who participated and how widely; (3) What form the action took; (4) How the colonial government responded. After completing the table, write your evaluative paragraph: state which approach you judge most consequential, give two pieces of evidence from the table, and acknowledge one limitation of your judgement.
format_of_output: A completed four-column comparison table with one row per approach.
A three-to-four sentence evaluative paragraph naming the most consequential approach, citing two pieces of table evidence, and acknowledging one limitation.
assessment_items.inclusivity: Students who find table construction difficult may instead produce two annotated columns in list form. The evaluative paragraph requirement remains the same for all students.

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: Students apply analytical and evaluative skills to compare four historically distinct forms of resistance, moving beyond recalling events to judging their relative impact on the colonial government's calculations.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: The four columns direct students to populate the table with content evidence before they write evaluatively, preventing the common error of making an unsupported claim. The paragraph's requirement to cite table evidence and acknowledge a limitation pushes students beyond simple assertion toward reasoned argument.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong responses populate all four table columns with accurate chapter detail, write a paragraph that names a specific colonial response as evidence of impact, and acknowledge a genuine limitation (e.g. the Kuka movement's regional reach vs its suppression). Weak responses list leaders' names without characterising the form of action, or write a paragraph that merely restates the table without making an evaluative claim.
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: A comparison table is the most natural demonstration vehicle for this LO because the skill is placing multiple simultaneous forms of resistance side by side to assess their relative impact — exactly the analytical operation a table structure externalises and makes visible. The teacher may substitute any other format from the menu (cause-effect map, structured discussion prompt with written output, source analysis task) if better suited to the class.

competency.competency_text: Interpret primary and secondary sources to construct historical understanding.

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can read a period newspaper extract to decode the political language used to advance nationalist goals.
assessment_items.question_text: The September 1906 Bande Mataram article argued for 'absolute national autonomy' rather than using the word 'independence'. Which of the following best explains why the editors made this linguistic choice?

options.label: A
options.text: The Calcutta Congress session of 1906 had formally prohibited the use of the word 'independence' in Congress publications.

options.label: B
options.text: The editors genuinely believed that India should remain within the British Empire and were not yet calling for full separation.

options.label: C
options.text: The editors were translating a Bengali phrase that had no exact English equivalent and 'absolute national autonomy' was the closest available rendering.

options.label: D
options.text: The word 'independence' carried a direct legal and political risk of sedition charges, while 'absolute national autonomy' conveyed the same goal with enough ambiguity to avoid immediate suppression.

what_each_option_reveals.B: Misreads strategic language as literal belief — confuses the editors' tactical use of ambiguity with genuine ideological moderation.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Fabricates a translation explanation not supported by the chapter — the paper was published in English and the phrase was a deliberate political choice.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Invents a Congress prohibition with no basis in the chapter — the 1906 session's ambiguity about 'Swaraj' was quite different from a prohibition on 'independence'.

competency.competency_text: Interpret primary and secondary sources to construct historical understanding.

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can interpret a protest letter from a public figure to reconstruct the moral and political critique it makes of state violence.
assessment_items.question_text: In his letter returning his knighthood after the Jallianwala Bagh massacre, Rabindranath Tagore wrote that the rulers 'congratulated themselves'. What did he mean by this phrase?

options.label: A
options.text: He meant that British officials had publicly celebrated Dyer's action as a successful display of imperial authority, revealing their moral indifference to Indian lives.

options.label: B
options.text: He meant that Indian Congress leaders had thanked the British for organizing a fair investigation through a majority-British inquiry committee.

options.label: C
options.text: He meant that the British government had congratulated itself on granting a public inquiry into the massacre, which Tagore considered an adequate response.

options.label: D
options.text: He meant that the British officials had praised the restraint shown by Brigadier-General Dyer in limiting the number of rounds fired.

assessment_items.inclusivity: Students may be asked to read the question aloud in pairs before answering if processing written English is a challenge.

what_each_option_reveals.D: Inverts Tagore's critique — he was not praising restraint but condemning the approval of the massacre; confuses the direction of the moral argument.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Conflates Tagore's sarcasm with a literal reading — he was critiquing the inquiry's inadequacy, not praising it as adequate.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Attributes 'congratulations' to Indian leaders rather than British officials, and misattributes the inquiry's composition — the chapter says it was British-dominated.

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can compare the demands in a resolution text to identify the political principles it asserts and the compromises it implies.
assessment_items.question_text: The Lahore resolution of December 1929 declared it the inalienable right of the Indian people to freedom and the right to alter or abolish an oppressive government. Identify two political principles this resolution asserts, and explain what the use of the word 'inalienable' adds to the demand.
expected_elements: Names two distinct principles: (1) the right to complete independence / Purna Swaraj; (2) the right to alter or abolish an oppressive government.
Explains that 'inalienable' means the right cannot be taken away or bargained away — it does not depend on British consent or concession.
Connects the language to the shift from earlier positions (dominion status, self-government within the Empire) to an unconditional demand.

competency.competency_text: Explain the reasons behind harmony and conflict among communities and their impact on society.

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can explain how a deliberate colonial strategy of communal division simultaneously produced both inter-community solidarity and lasting antagonism.
assessment_items.chapter_section: The 1905 Partition of Bengal and National Awakening
assessment_items.question_text: Viceroy Curzon's 1905 partition of Bengal split the largely Muslim east from the largely Hindu west. Which row in the table correctly pairs a community response to the partition with the long-term consequence the chapter identifies? Refer to the table provided.

options.label: A
options.text: Row 1

options.label: B
options.text: Row 2

options.label: C
options.text: Row 3

options.label: D
options.text: Row 4

assessment_items.visual_stimulus:
Community Response | Long-term consequence identified by the chapter
Swadeshi and boycott campaigns; singing of Vande Mataram; tying of rakhis as Hindu-Muslim unity | The partition permanently ended communal conflict in Bengal, and Hindu-Muslim relations remained harmonious thereafter
Most Muslim leaders defended the partition because the new eastern province gave Muslims a majority; Congress leaders and others united across communities in opposition | Both effects occurred simultaneously — sharpened communal division and a national awakening of protests and solidarity gestures
The tying of rakhis and the Swadeshi movement convinced the colonial government to reverse the partition immediately in 1905 | Communal harmony was fully restored and no further Hindu-Muslim tensions emerged from this episode
Aurobindo Ghose founded the Bengal National College as a direct response to the partition | The college's founding resolved the communal crisis by providing an alternative to government education for both communities
assessment_items.inclusivity: Students unfamiliar with tabular formats may be directed to read each row as a sentence pair before making their selection.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Misreads the chapter's account of consequences — the partition did not end communal conflict; it sharpened it alongside producing solidarity gestures.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Confuses the timeline — the partition was annulled in 1911, not immediately in 1905, and communal tensions persisted long after.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Conflates the National Council of Education's founding with a resolution of the communal crisis — the chapter presents these as separate developments with distinct purposes.

competency.competency_text: Explain the reasons behind harmony and conflict among communities and their impact on society.

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can assess the conditions under which a cross-community political alliance forms, fractures, and leaves a contested legacy.
assessment_items.question_text: The 1920 Khilafat–Non-Cooperation alliance between the Congress and Khilafat leaders initially increased Muslim participation in the national movement. Which statement best evaluates why this alliance left a contested legacy?

options.label: A
options.text: The alliance achieved temporary Hindu-Muslim cooperation but was built on a religious cause external to India; when Turkey abolished the caliphate in 1922 and 1924 the movement collapsed, leaving behind a reinforced sense of separateness and subsequent communal riots.

options.label: B
options.text: The alliance failed because Gandhi refused to allow Khilafat leaders to speak at Congress sessions, creating personal resentment.

options.label: C
options.text: The alliance failed because the All-India Muslim League opposed it from the start and prevented Muslim participation.

options.label: D
options.text: The alliance was a complete success because it permanently resolved Hindu-Muslim tensions and the Khilafat Movement's goals were fully achieved.

what_each_option_reveals.B: Fabricates a personal conflict not mentioned in the chapter — Gandhi actively sought the alliance with the Ali brothers and Maulana Azad.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Ignores the chapter's explicit account of the debated legacy — subsequent riots and a reinforced sense of separateness — by treating a temporary unity as a permanent resolution.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Reverses the chapter's account — the League did not uniformly oppose the alliance; several Muslim leaders and organisations supported it, and the chapter's critique came from within Congress (Jinnah) and from Muslim leaders who objected to linking Indian Muslim loyalty to a Turkish religious authority.

Notes that this fear affected even those who had opposed partition, shifting the political calculation toward accepting partition as a way to stop the violence.
Connects the violence to the British decision to hasten transfer of power.

competency.competency_text: Assess the influence of political institutions on Indian society.

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can assess the reach and limitations of the early Congress as a political institution in representing diverse Indian grievances.
assessment_items.chapter_section: The Rise of the Indian National Congress
assessment_items.question_text: At its founding in 1885, the Indian National Congress passed resolutions seeking dialogue, greater Indian participation in governance, and civil rights reforms. The colonial government largely ignored these resolutions. Which assessment of the early Congress as a political institution is best supported by the chapter?

options.label: A
options.text: The Congress succeeded in its founding mission because it united Moderates and Nationalists into a single voice that the colonial government was forced to recognise.

options.label: B
options.text: The Congress was a purely colonial creation, since it was founded by A.O. Hume, a British officer, and therefore represented British rather than Indian interests.

options.label: C
options.text: The Congress was an effective institution because its seventy-two delegates from diverse regions and religions proved the colonial government could not dismiss Indian demands.

options.label: D
options.text: The Congress was an institution that opened a legitimate space for political representation but was limited in reach — mostly Anglicised upper classes — and in impact, since the colonial government ignored its resolutions and conceded only minor reforms.

what_each_option_reveals.C: Overstates the Congress's effectiveness by equating diverse attendance with political impact — the chapter explicitly states the colonial government largely ignored its resolutions.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Oversimplifies Hume's role — the chapter says Hume had become critical of colonial policies and brought together like-minded Indians; the Congress's agenda was nationalist, not colonial.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Confuses the founding period with later developments — the Surat split of 1907 shows Moderates and Nationalists were not united, and unity was only partially restored with the 1916 Lucknow session.

competency.competency_text: Assess the influence of political institutions on Indian society.

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can evaluate how a colonial institution's deliberate exclusion of Indian voices shaped the character of Indian political resistance.
assessment_items.question_text: The Simon Commission arrived in India in 1927 to study constitutional reform but had no Indian members. Which statement best evaluates the political consequence of this exclusion?

options.label: A
options.text: The exclusion confirmed in practice what the independence movement had argued in principle — that the British were unwilling to consult Indians about their own future — and intensified calls for complete self-rule rather than incremental reform.

options.label: B
options.text: The exclusion had little political impact because Indian leaders were already focused on the Salt March rather than constitutional reform.

options.label: C
options.text: The exclusion led moderate Congress leaders to collaborate with the Simon Commission as the only available path to gradual self-government.

options.label: D
options.text: The exclusion was irrelevant because the Motilal Nehru Committee had already proposed a constitution that made the Simon Commission unnecessary.

what_each_option_reveals.B: Creates a false chronology — the Salt March was 1930, three years after the Simon Commission's arrival; students who select this are confusing the sequence of events.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Reverses the chapter's account — the response was 'Simon Go Back' rallies and black flags, not collaboration; the Nehru Report came from the Congress independently, not in cooperation with the Commission.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Conflates the Nehru Committee's Dominion status report (a Congress response) with making the Commission irrelevant — the chapter presents them as parallel tracks, not substitutes.

competency.competency_text: Assess the influence of political institutions on Indian society.

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can assess how an institutional split altered the political options available to different factions within the independence movement.
assessment_items.question_text: At the 1907 Surat session, the Moderates and the Nationalist faction led by Tilak, Lala Lajpat Rai and Aurobindo Ghose split into two separate sessions. Explain how this institutional split changed the political options available to each faction in their dealings with the colonial government.
expected_elements: Identifies what each faction wanted: Moderates sought gradual self-government within the Empire; Nationalists demanded nothing less than independence.
Explains that a split weakened the Congress as a single negotiating body, since the colonial government could treat the two factions differently.

Notes that the Moderates, by returning to minor-concession politics, gave the British a partner willing to accept less; the Nationalists, outside the Congress structure, had greater ideological freedom but less institutional leverage.
Makes an evaluative point about whether the split strengthened or weakened the independence movement overall.
