competency.competency_text: Identify continuities in cultural and civilisational traditions across periods of political change.

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can identify how cultural symbols and spiritual traditions carried forward across political changes to sustain nationalist consciousness.
assessment_items.question_text: Bande Mataram was composed by Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay in 1875, set to music and sung by Rabindranath Tagore at the 1896 Calcutta Congress session, sung in the streets during the 1905 anti-partition protests, and adopted as India's National Song by the Constituent Assembly in 1950. What does this seventy-five-year journey of the song tell us about the relationship between cultural expression and political mobilisation?

options.label: A
options.text: Cultural expressions created in one political context can be reactivated in successive political moments to give a movement emotional and symbolic force that formal resolutions alone cannot provide.

options.label: B
options.text: The repeated use of Bande Mataram in different contexts shows that cultural symbols lose their political meaning the more widely they are used.

options.label: C
options.text: The song's adoption by the Constituent Assembly proved that Bankim Chandra's political views were fully endorsed by the new Indian government.

options.label: D
options.text: The song's journey shows that all cultural expressions eventually become official state symbols, regardless of their original political intention.

what_each_option_reveals.D: Overgeneralises from one case to a universal claim — the chapter does not suggest all cultural expressions become state symbols; this confuses a specific trajectory with a rule.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Conflates the adoption of the song with an endorsement of the author's views — the chapter does not make this connection, and it misunderstands what adopting a national song means.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Inverts the chapter's account — Vande Mataram's repeated use in different contexts is presented as evidence of sustained political resonance, not dilution of meaning.

competency.competency_text: Identify continuities in cultural and civilisational traditions across periods of political change.

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can trace how a cultural symbol composed decades earlier was reactivated as a vehicle for political resistance.
assessment_items.chapter_section: The 1905 Partition of Bengal and National Awakening
assessment_items.question_text: In the streets of Calcutta during the anti-partition protests of 1905, crowds sang Vande Mataram until the colonial authorities banned it. The song had been composed thirty years earlier in a novel set in an eighteenth-century famine. What does its reappearance in 1905 street protests illustrate about how cultural symbols work in political movements?

options.label: A
options.text: A cultural symbol created in one historical crisis can be reactivated by a later generation facing a different crisis, drawing on accumulated emotional meaning to bind a diverse group together in resistance.

options.label: B
options.text: A cultural symbol that is officially banned gains no additional political significance — suppression is an effective way to remove it from public consciousness.

options.label: C
options.text: Cultural symbols are only effective when they are newly created for a specific political moment; older symbols lose their emotional power.

options.label: D
options.text: The use of Vande Mataram in 1905 shows that literary fiction is a more reliable source of political mobilisation than formal party organisation.

what_each_option_reveals.C: Contradicts the specific evidence — Vande Mataram was thirty years old and deeply effective; this option reflects a presentist assumption not supported by the chapter.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Contradicts the chapter — banning the song in the streets made it more politically charged, not less; this confuses suppression with erasure.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Overclaims from one example — the chapter does not suggest fiction is universally more effective than party organisation; this conflates a specific case with a general rule.

competency.competency_text: Recognise patterns of prejudice, discrimination and exclusion and their social consequences.

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can categorise the systematic forms of racial and economic discrimination embedded in colonial law and explain their cumulative social effect.
assessment_items.question_text: The colonial government maintained several forms of systematic discrimination against Indians after 1858. Which of the following correctly identifies two legally embedded forms of racial discrimination described in the chapter?

options.label: A
options.text: British-majority juries that were lenient towards European crimes, and the 1878 Arms Act barring Indians from keeping arms.

options.label: B
options.text: The exclusion of Indians from positions in the Indian National Congress and the banning of the Vernacular Press in 1885.

options.label: C
options.text: The partition of Bengal in 1905 and the founding of the All-India Muslim League, which together excluded Hindus from eastern Bengal.

options.label: D
options.text: The Rowlatt Act of 1919 and the Simon Commission of 1927, both of which excluded Indians from decision-making.

what_each_option_reveals.B: Contains two inaccuracies — the Congress did not exclude Indians (it was founded to represent them); the Vernacular Press Act was 1878, not 1885.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Correctly identifies discriminatory measures but from a later period (1919, 1927) rather than the post-1858 immediate context of the Royal Proclamation section.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Confuses administrative and political events with legally embedded racial discrimination — partition and the Muslim League's founding were not discriminatory laws of the 1858 type.

competency.competency_text: Analyse how colonial economic policies shaped production, consumption and capital in Indian society.

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can explain how colonial taxation and trade policies disrupted Indian production and drove recurring famine.
assessment_items.question_text: The chapter states that after 1858 heavy land taxes produced severe famines and discontent, and that local industries could not compete with cheap British manufactures. Which of the following best explains the connection between these two problems?

options.label: A
options.text: Cheap British manufactures caused famines directly by reducing food production, since Indian farmers switched from growing food to producing raw materials for British factories.

options.label: B
options.text: Heavy land taxes forced peasants to sell their produce to pay taxes rather than storing food, while cheap British imports undercut Indian artisans, leaving both groups without a reliable income during crop failures.

options.label: C
options.text: Heavy land taxes were the only cause of famine; cheap British manufactures actually helped Indians by lowering the cost of goods they needed to buy.

options.label: D
options.text: Land taxes and cheap British manufactures were unrelated problems affecting different groups of Indians — peasants and industrial workers respectively — with no shared cause.

what_each_option_reveals.D: Misses the chapter's systemic framing — colonial economic policy affected multiple sectors simultaneously and the two problems reinforced each other; treating them as unrelated is a compartmentalisation error.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Overstates the causal chain — while raw material extraction was part of colonial economy, the chapter attributes famine to heavy land taxation, not to a switch from food to raw material production caused by cheap manufactures.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Applies a free-market logic the chapter explicitly rejects — cheap British manufactures undermined Indian industries rather than benefiting Indian consumers overall, and land taxes are presented as part of a broader extractive system, not the sole cause of famine.

competency.competency_text: Analyse how colonial economic policies shaped production, consumption and capital in Indian society.

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can explain why a state monopoly over a basic commodity made salt a potent symbol for challenging colonial economic control.
assessment_items.question_text: Gandhi chose to challenge the colonial government's salt monopoly for the Civil Disobedience Movement rather than, for example, challenging the cotton import tax. Which explanation best captures why salt was a more effective choice?

options.label: A
options.text: Gandhi chose salt because the British had admitted the salt tax was unfair in the Simon Commission report, giving the movement a legal basis for protest.

options.label: B
options.text: Salt was chosen because it was a luxury good, and challenging a tax on luxuries would appeal to wealthy Congress supporters who could afford to boycott foreign cotton but not salt.

options.label: C
options.text: Salt was produced only in coastal regions, so a march to the coast would attract more media coverage than a protest at an inland mill.

options.label: D
options.text: The colonial government held a monopoly on salt production and taxed it heavily; salt was needed by every Indian regardless of region, religion or income, making the monopoly a daily, personal experience of colonial economic control for the entire population.

what_each_option_reveals.C: Focuses on a tactical detail (coastal location and media) while missing the economic and social logic — the chapter explains the choice through monopoly and universality, not media strategy.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Inverts the chapter's account — salt was chosen precisely because it was a basic necessity for everyone, especially the poor, not a luxury for the wealthy.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Fabricates a concession not in the chapter — the Simon Commission report is not described as admitting the salt tax was unfair, and Gandhi's choice of salt pre-dates the Commission's report.

competency.competency_text: Recognise India's contributions to global knowledge and civilisation and their significance.

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can articulate how Indian thinkers presented their civilisational traditions to a global audience and explain the domestic confidence this generated.
assessment_items.question_text: At the 1893 Parliament of the World's Religions in Chicago, Swami Vivekananda made a powerful defence of India's civilisation and returned urging Indians to 'Arise, awake, and stop not till the goal is reached.' He also advised Jamsetji Tata to create what became the Indian Institute of Science. How do these two actions together illustrate a contribution to national confidence?

options.label: A
options.text: Vivekananda believed Indian civilisation was superior to Western civilisation in every respect and therefore rejected all Western science, including the science on which the Indian Institute of Science was based.

options.label: B
options.text: Vivekananda showed that defending India's spiritual tradition internationally and encouraging scientific institution-building at home were complementary rather than contradictory, countering the colonial argument that Indian civilisation had nothing to contribute to the modern world.

options.label: C
options.text: Vivekananda's Chicago speech was primarily an attempt to convert Western audiences to Hinduism, while his advice to Tata was unrelated to the independence movement.

options.label: D
options.text: Vivekananda's contribution to national confidence came only through his spiritual teaching and had no connection to practical economic or scientific development in India.

what_each_option_reveals.C: Misreads both actions — the chapter presents the Chicago speech as a defence of India's civilisation (not a conversion effort) and links the IIS advice to Vivekananda's broader role in building national confidence.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Contradicts the chapter — Vivekananda 'encouraged science' and advised Tata, demonstrating that he embraced modern science while rejecting 'blind imitation of the West'; the option conflates selective critique with wholesale rejection.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Artificially separates spiritual and practical contributions — the chapter presents both the Chicago speech and the IIS advice as part of the same effort to overcome Indian self-doubt and colonial dependency.
